analysis.one_liner: Bars Medicare drug plans and PBMs from excluding pharmacies willing to accept the plan's contract terms.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote; it sat in the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees from September 2023 until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) are middlemen that run prescription drug plans for insurers, and they decide which pharmacies are 'in network.' The bill would change Medicare Part D rules so that any pharmacy willing to accept a plan's standard contract terms must be allowed into that plan's network, and it directs the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to define what counts as reasonable contract terms by January 1, 2026. The goal is to stop plans from dropping local and independent pharmacies, which can force Medicare patients to switch pharmacies or travel farther to fill prescriptions. The bill never got a vote; it sat in committee for the rest of the 118th Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who use local or independent pharmacies, especially in rural areas and neighborhoods where plans have narrowed their networks and patients must switch pharmacies or travel farther. Community and independent pharmacies benefit directly, because they can no longer be excluded from a plan's network when they accept its terms.

how_it_helps.text: Plans and PBMs could no longer exclude pharmacies that agree to the plan's standard terms, so beneficiaries keep access to their local pharmacy.

It forces the Department of Health and Human Services to set standards for 'reasonable and relevant' contract terms by January 1, 2026, replacing one-sided contracts with federally defined ground rules.
By ending exclusionary networks, it protects smaller community pharmacies, which often cannot survive losing a major plan's customers.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and Medicare drug plan sponsors bear the cost: they lose the ability to build exclusive networks and use exclusion as leverage to negotiate lower reimbursement rates, which could mean some higher plan costs passed on to premiums or taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: Any-willing-pharmacy rules cut the other way on price: broader networks mean each pharmacy fills fewer prescriptions and plans lose their main bargaining chip for lower reimbursement rates, so some savings could shift into premiums paid by beneficiaries and the federal government.

The bill does not ban PBMs or cap their fees; it only requires open networks, so the middleman business model it targets would continue under somewhat tighter rules, with new standards not required until January 1, 2026.
The Secretary gets broad discretion to define what contract terms are 'reasonable and relevant,' leaving the practical effect dependent on future regulations the bill does not specify.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but targeted: Medicare beneficiaries in places where the biggest drug plans have narrowed their pharmacy networks would get more choice and shorter trips to fill prescriptions, and independent pharmacies would keep doors open that they otherwise might close. The cost is honest but modest: opening networks to any willing pharmacy chips away at the bargaining power plans and PBMs use to negotiate drug prices, so some savings could erode or show up in premiums. The bill is a narrow, reasonable fix rather than a structural overhaul of PBM middleman fees, and it never got far enough to be tested either way.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in committee and its Health subcommittee without ever getting a markup or a floor vote, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 12, 2023 by Rep. Buddy Carter and referred to two House committees, Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, first in September 2023 and again in December 2024, and never advanced further.
Neither full committee ever held a markup on the bill, and the full House never voted on it.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and the large drug plans that rely on them, who keep the power to build exclusive pharmacy networks and set contract terms on their own. Independent pharmacies and Medicare beneficiaries in areas with limited pharmacy choice are no better off.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced, referred it to its Health Subcommittee in September 2023 and again in December 2024, and never brought it to a markup or a vote.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of second referral (shares jurisdiction over Medicare)

against.name: Pharmacy benefit managers and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: PBMs and their trade group have publicly opposed any-willing-pharmacy and PBM-network regulation across federal and state legislatures, arguing it raises drug plan costs.

sides.party_line_note: Support was evenly bipartisan: a Republican sponsor with 9 cosponsors split 5 Democrats and 4 Republicans, and the bill died in committee rather than failing along party lines.

industries.note: PBMs build and control pharmacy networks for Medicare drug plans; this bill takes away their power to exclude pharmacies and subjects their contract terms to federal standards, cutting into the leverage at the center of their business model.

Independent pharmacies are the main beneficiaries: they could no longer be dropped from a plan's network even when they accept its terms, which protects their prescription volume and their patients' access to them.

industries.industry: Medicare prescription drug plans and insurers
industries.note: Plan sponsors would have to open their networks to any willing pharmacy, giving up exclusivity deals but no longer solely accountable for network decisions PBMs make on their behalf.
Chains are already in nearly every network, so they gain little; they do gain if open-network rules raise reimbursement rates by increasing competition for pharmacies.
